summary: A list of blocks (01)^x (1)^y in which every 1-block shrinks by 2 and every 01-block grows by 1 per sweep; an empty 1-block merges its neighbours by a zigzag, and a merge at the left end halts the machine if its left block is too short (proved). An exact block machine, proved in Lean, runs it to 10^18 steps: at all 49 left-end merges the right block was at most 0.35 times the left one once the left block had 50 pairs (0.6 at the tiny early ones).
title: What is known about 1RB1LF_1RC1RB_1RD0RB_0LE0LF_---1LD_0LE1LA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_1RC1RB_1RD0RB_0LE0LF_---1LD_0LE1LA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Open, with the way to halt pinned down and the run followed exactly to 1018 steps. The tape is a list of blocks (01)^x (1)^y; Lean proves (kernel) that a merge at the left end halts the machine when the right block has at least two pairs more than the left one, and that a run-length block machine follows the Turing machine exactly from blank tape. Its C twin finds no halt in 1018 steps: at all 49 merges at the left end with a left block of 50 pairs or more the right block was at most 0.35 times the left one (0.6 at the tiny early ones).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 41,232 cells have been visited and 23,700 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.505). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.505).

claims.title: The merge zigzag
claims.text: L (01)^(a+1) A>0 1 (11)^n 0 (01)^(k+1) R becomes L (01)^a A>0 1 (11)^(n+2) 0 (01)^k R in 4n+10 steps, for every a, n, k and every tape L, R; iterated j times by induction.

claims.title: A short left block halts the machine
claims.text: At the left end, 0^∞ 1 1 1 (01)^a A>0 1 (11)^n 0 (01)^(a+k+2) R halts, for every a, n, k and R: the zigzag uses up the left block and E reads the blank cell at the left end.

claims.title: The sweep law
claims.text: Between two visits of the left end, every block (01)^x becomes (01)^(x+1) and every block (1)^y becomes (1)^(y-2): 289,603 checks in the first 1010 steps, no exception.
claims.where: scratch analysis of the C run (py/analyze.py)

claims.title: The merge law
claims.text: When a block (1)^y between (01)^a and (01)^b (1)^c runs out, the zigzag leaves (01)^(a-b) (1)^(4b+c); seen at every merge of the first 1010 steps.

claims.title: The left block stays about 3 times longer
claims.text: At the 23 merges at the left end in the first 10<sup>10</sup> steps the left block was 2.9 to 4.3 times the right one (last: 30,587 against 9,616), and a longer run of the left end alone found a 24th at about 1.2·10<sup>10</sup> steps with 45,881 against 12,860 (ratio 3.6); at all 1,497 merges with a right block of at least 15 pairs the ratio was at least 2.9.

claims.title: An exact abstract machine for the whole run
claims.text: The tape cut into blocks of two cells, each side of the head run-length coded: one step of this block machine runs the Turing machine on the block the head faces (two 48-entry window tables, each entry checked by rfl) and crosses a whole run of equal blocks at once when the head leaves a block in the state it entered with. Every block-machine step is a run of the Turing machine, a block-machine halt is a halt, and the empty block configuration is the blank tape.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1,199,390 steps
claims.text: 30,000 steps of the block machine from blank tape, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 124,890,717,366 steps
claims.text: 18,000,000 steps of the block machine, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>18</sup> steps
claims.text: The block machine in C (c/msim.c, the same window tables and run crossing; it agrees with Lean's evaluation of mrun on the step counts after 1,000, 4,635,164 and 18,000,000 block steps) runs 1018 steps in about 8 minutes without a halt.

claims.title: 49 merges at the left end, none close to halting
claims.text: In the first 10<sup>18</sup> steps there are 49 merges at the left end; the right block was at most 0.6 times the left one at the tiny early merges (3 to 13 pairs), at most 0.346 once the left block had 50 pairs, and between 0.22 and 0.34 once it had 100 (halting needs about 1). At every merge inside the tape the left block was at least 1.67 times the right one, and at least 2.89 times when the right block had 15 pairs or more.

claims.title: Each left-end merge protects the next one
claims.text: With X0, X1, X2 the first three blocks of pairs at a left-end merge, the next left-end merge is safe if X0 − X1 > X2, because X0 − X1 never decreases between two left-end merges (an argument from the sweep and merge laws; checked at 11,085,706 consecutive left-end visits to 10<sup>15</sup> steps, one exception at step 2,871 with blocks of at most 10 pairs). At every left-end merge with X0 ≥ 100 up to 2·10<sup>17</sup> steps (47 merges), (X0 − X1)/X2 was at least 5.8.

claims.title: A roughly self-similar cascade
claims.text: From one left-end merge to the next the left block grows by a factor of 1.3 to 1.5 (often exactly 3/2 up to rounding: 571,835, 857,753, 1,286,629) and follows X0' = X0 + X1 + m2 (±1). Each block of pairs is longer than all later ones together at every left-end visit (smallest ratio 1.65 to 10<sup>14</sup> steps), but neither this nor any simple inequality on the blocks survives both sweeps and merges, so it is not an inductive invariant.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The machine halts if a merge at the left end ever meets a right block not shorter than the left one (by 2). The block machine of lean/Macro.lean is exact, so a halt would show up in it; a proof of non-halting needs an invariant of the whole cascade of merges, which is not known.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet, but the one way it can stop is known, and the run has been followed exactly for 1018 steps. The tape is a row of blocks: runs of 01 pairs that grow and runs of 1s that shrink, a little at each sweep of the head. When a run of 1s is used up, its two neighbours merge in a zigzag, and a merge at the left end halts the machine if its left block is too short. So far the right block has never been even half as long as the left one.

facts.text: A left-end merge with a right block 2 or more pairs longer than the left one halts (Lean).
A run-length block machine follows the machine step for step from blank tape (Lean).
No halt in the C block machine; 49 merges at the left end.
Right block over left block at every left-end merge with a left block of 50 pairs or more (halting needs about 1).
Steps without a halt proved in Lean by evaluating the block machine; 1.2·10<sup>6</sup> by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.505). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.505).
After 109 steps the tape spans 41,232 cells (16,214 left of the start, 14,009 right), with a density of 1s of 0.575.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A row of growing and shrinking blocks
html: Stop the machine each time the head is at the left end of the tape (in state A). The tape then always reads
(01)^x0 (1)^y1 (01)^x1 (1)^y2 (01)^x2 … (1)^yk (01)^xk · short tail
for example, at step 9,999,886,792:

Between two visits of the left end the head runs right (state B turns every 01 into 10 and passes over 1s), bounces near the right end and comes back (A and F walk over 1s, E and D over pairs). The net effect of one round trip is simple:

blockafter one round trip
(01)^x(01)^(x+1)
(1)^y(1)^(y−2)

Each boundary moves two cells to the right, so the length of every pair of blocks, 2x + y, stays the same. The short tail at the right end keeps making new small blocks; the same tail patterns recur over and over, so the small blocks are recycled the way low digits of a counter are.

Each separator between two blocks of pairs lives the same life: 1^y → 1^(y−2) → … → 1 → [0] → [10] → merge, where [0] is a single 0 cell and [10] the cells 1 0. The head going right turns back at the first [0], so for one round trip the part of the tape beyond it is not swept. A stretch at the left end ((x) stands for (01)^x):

steptape at the left end
11,213(41) 1 (13) 1^5 (6) 1^3 (3) …
11,502(41) [0] (14) 1^3 (7) 1 (3) …
11,671(42) [10] (13) 1^3 (7) 1 (3) …
12,950(29) 1^55 (6) 1^9 (3) …

In the last line the merge has happened: 42 − 13 = 29 pairs are left of the new block of ones, which has 4·13 + 3 = 55 cells.

sections.heading: When a run of 1s runs out: the merge
html: The 1-block with the smallest y empties first. Then the head stops making full round trips and zigzags on the spot: each zigzag takes one pair from the block on the left and one from the block on the right and adds four 1s in between,
(01)^(a+1) A>0 1 (11)^n 0 (01)^(k+1) → (01)^a A>0 1 (11)^(n+2) 0 (01)^k   (4n+10 steps)
(proved in Lean for all a, n, k). When the right block (01)^b is used up the zigzag stops and normal sweeping resumes:
(01)^a [empty] (01)^b (1)^c → (01)^(a−b) (1)^(4b+c)
Example (step 438,516): (01)^261 1 0 (01)^82 (1)^81 becomes (01)^180 (1)^409: 261 − 82 = 179 plus the pair gained on that round trip, and 4·82 + 81 = 409.

sections.heading: A block machine proved to follow the machine
html: The description above is a reading of a simpler object that Lean checks completely. Cut the tape into blocks of two cells and store each side of the head as a list of runs (block, count), so 01 01 01 … is one entry 01^x. One step of this block machine looks up what the machine does on the block in front of the head (it leaves the block to the right or to the left in some state, having rewritten it; 48 cases for each side, each one checked by Lean). If the head leaves on the far side in the state it came in with, it would do the same on every copy, so the whole run of equal blocks is crossed in one step.

Lean proves for every configuration that each block-machine step is a run of the real machine and that a block-machine halt is a real halt, starting from the blank tape. So the block machine is an exact abstract machine for the whole run, not an approximation: the blocks (01)^x and (1)^y are its runs 01^x, 10^x and 11^m.

It is fast because a sweep over a block of a million pairs is a single step. Evaluated inside Lean it certifies 124,890,717,366 steps without a halt; the same machine written in C reaches 1010 steps in 0.03 seconds and 1018 in about eight minutes.

sections.heading: The one way to halt
html: The merge needs a > b: the block on the left must outlast the block on the right. If the left block runs out first, the zigzag walks into whatever lies further left. At the left end of the tape that is 1 1 1 and then blank tape, and Lean proves (kernel only, every a, n, k) that
0^∞ 1 1 1 (01)^a A>0 1 (11)^n 0 (01)^(a+k+2) …  halts:

after a zigzags the left block is gone, the head runs left over the ones in state F, reads the blank cell, and E on a 0 is the halting transition. Simulating real tapes with the left block shortened confirms it: with the right block 28, every left block up to 28 halts.
So does the left block always win? At the 23 left-end merges of the first 1010 steps the left block was 2.9 to 4.3 times the right one:

Internal merges behave the same way (ratio at least 2.9 at all 1,497 merges whose right block has 15 or more pairs). A proof of non-halting would need an invariant that keeps this ratio above 1 through every merge and every block the tail creates; an internal merge with a short left block would not halt at once (the zigzag walks into the 1-block further left), so the left end is the critical place.

There is also a margin for the future. Right after a left-end merge the new left block is X0 − X1 and the new right block is the next block X2; until the next left-end merge the difference between them can only grow (both gain a pair per sweep and merges further right only shorten the right one). So a merge with X0 − X1 > X2 makes the next one safe, and in the run (X0 − X1)/X2 was always at least 5.8 (to 2·1017 steps).

sections.heading: Why this is not yet a proof
html: Follow each block of ones in coordinates that move with it: its left end minus the time and its right end plus the time. These two numbers stay fixed between merges. A merge mirrors the left end of the next block about the point where the vanished block closed, and the machine halts exactly when such a mirror image passes the left end of the tape. New small blocks keep arriving from the right end, and merges cascade from the right towards the left, the left block growing by a factor of about 1.3 to 1.5 each time (often exactly 3/2 up to rounding).

So the question is about a deterministic cascade that looks roughly the same at every scale, like the Collatz-type questions behind other holdouts. Simple inequalities do not close up: each block of pairs is longer than all later ones together holds throughout the run and survives merges, but the sweeps break it; the blocks of pairs get shorter to the right survives sweeps but not merges. A proof of non-halting needs an invariant of the whole cascade.
